cards.explanation: The answer is unintentionally. The LORD says to deal with “…one who sins unintentionally against any of the LORD’s commandments…” (Leviticus 4:2). This is the sin nobody meant to do, like sitting on your own sunglasses. Nobody saw it coming, but it still counts, friends. Notice the LORD makes a way for it anyway.

The answer is the people. When the anointed priest sins, he is “…bringing guilt on the people…” (Leviticus 4:3). The priest sins, and the guilt lands on the people. That's a lot of weight for one pair of shoulders, friends. It's like a delivery guy who trips on the porch step and the whole box of cookies goes down with him. His stumble isn't just his.

The answer is when they become aware of the sin. The text says “…when they become aware of the sin they have committed, then the assembly must bring a young bull as a sin offering…” (Leviticus 4:14). Becoming aware is the cue the verse gives, friends. No calendar needed for this one.

The answer is the elders of the congregation. The text says “The elders of the congregation are to lay their hands on the bull’s head before the LORD…” (Leviticus 4:15). The elders are the ones the text names for the hand-laying on the assembly's bull, friends. Then it shall be slaughtered before the LORD.

The answer is False. The elders lay their hands on the bull's head (Leviticus 4:15), but they don't make the atonement. The text says “…the priest will make atonement on their behalf, and they will be forgiven.” (Leviticus 4:20). Everybody has a part, friends, and nobody takes somebody else's job.

The answer is forgiven. The text says “…the priest will make atonement on their behalf, and they will be forgiven.” (Leviticus 4:20). Look at where the verse ends up, friends. The assembly is forgiven. I'd hang that one on my bakery wall.

The answer is True. The text says “When a leader sins unintentionally and does what is prohibited by any of the commandments of the LORD his God, he incurs guilt.” (Leviticus 4:22). Unintentional or not, the leader incurs guilt. The passage then says he brings an unblemished male goat when he becomes aware (Leviticus 4:23), and the priest makes atonement and he will be forgiven (Leviticus 4:26).

The answer is a pleasing aroma to the LORD. The priest burns the fat on the altar “…as a pleasing aroma to the LORD.” (Leviticus 4:31). Then comes the next part of the verse: “In this way the priest will make atonement for him, and he will be forgiven.” So the aroma goes up to the LORD, friends, and the one who brought the goat is forgiven.

The answer is True. The text says “If, however, he brings a lamb as a sin offering, he must bring an unblemished female.” (Leviticus 4:32). At the end of the lamb's steps it says, “In this way the priest will make atonement for him for the sin he has committed, and he will be forgiven.” (Leviticus 4:35). Goat or lamb, friends, the forgiveness is the same.

The answer is True. The text says that touching something unclean, “…even if he is unaware of it, he is unclean and guilty.” (Leviticus 5:2). The verse says he's unaware of it, friends. It's like finding a smear of dough on your sleeve you never saw. It was there the whole time.

The answer is False. The oath can be “…to do anything good or evil…” and “…even if he is unaware of it, when he realizes it, he is guilty in the matter.” (Leviticus 5:4). Words said in a rush still count, friends. Think twice before you promise.

The answer is confess. The text says “If someone incurs guilt in one of these ways, he must confess the sin he has committed…” (Leviticus 5:5). No dodging and no 'mistakes were made,' friends. Confess is the word the LORD uses. Then he brings his guilt offering to the LORD (Leviticus 5:6).

The answer is False. The text says that if he cannot afford a lamb, “…he may bring to the LORD as restitution for his sin two turtledoves or two young pigeons…” (Leviticus 5:7). A small budget doesn't shut the door, friends. The verse gives him another offering to bring instead of waiting for a lamb.

The answer is because it is a sin offering. That's the reason the text gives: “He must not put olive oil or frankincense on it, because it is a sin offering.” (Leviticus 5:11). The verse does the explaining for me, friends, and I love it when that happens.

The answer is any one of them. The text says “In this way the priest will make atonement for him for any of these sins he has committed, and he will be forgiven.” (Leviticus 5:13). Even the flour, the last option, reaches any of the sins the LORD listed, friends. A small offering, a full forgiveness.
